name: Action bias
statement: Where acting is the norm, people act even when doing nothing would serve them better, because a bad outcome after inaction feels worse than the same outcome after action.
meaning: The name covers two claims that are often run together. Patt and Zeckhauser's version is about wanting to affect an outcome: a penchant for action carried into areas where the reasons for it do not apply. Bar-Eli and colleagues' version is narrower and is the one usually quoted. It says the moral and emotional asymmetry that produces omission bias flips whenever acting, rather than sitting still, is what people expect. On that account there is no general preference for action and no general preference for inaction. There is a penalty attached to whichever choice departs from the norm, and the norm decides which way the bias points. Calling any of this a bias requires knowing what the better option was. In a contest where the other side adapts, that is a claim about equilibrium rather than about arithmetic, and it is where the argument has settled.

origin.note: "Action bias and environmental decisions" defined the term and tested it on hypothetical environmental choices. The famous evidence arrived seven years later with Bar-Eli and colleagues' penalty-kick study, which most retellings treat as the origin.

evidence: Patt and Zeckhauser's abstract states the idea and the finding together. Individuals have a penchant for action, often for good reasons, and action bias arises where that penchant is carried into areas the reasons do not cover. Given the ability to help one of two sites, their decision makers chose to foster improvement rather than prevent deterioration, although the framing made it arbitrary which site was improved and which preserved. They also report a strong form, in which people choose to reap gains even though they must impose losses. Bar-Eli, Azar, Ritov, Keidar-Levin and Schein supplied the case everybody cites. Three judges coded 311 televised penalty kicks, and exclusions for balls that missed the goal and for judge disagreement left 286. Goalkeepers jumped left in 49.3 percent of kicks, jumped right in 44.4 percent, and stayed in the centre in 6.3 percent. Kicks went left 32.2 percent of the time, centre 28.7 percent and right 39.2 percent. Jumping left stopped 14.2 percent of kicks and jumping right 12.6 percent, against 33.3 percent for staying. Jumping produced 36 stops and 232 goals, staying produced 6 stops and 12 goals, chi-square (1, N = 286) = 5.33, p = 0.02. A second study surveyed 32 of the 36 top professional goalkeepers in Israel. Twenty-five ranked jumping as more normal than staying and 7 ranked it the other way, chi-square (1, N = 32) = 10.13, p = 0.001. On the regret question 15 of the 32 gave the maximum rating to all three outcomes, leaving no room to compare them. Of the remaining 15, 11 said they would feel worse conceding after staying in the centre and 4 said the opposite, one-tailed binomial p = 0.059. The laboratory result behind the mechanism is Zeelenberg, van den Bos, van Dijk and Pieters. Across four experiments they manipulated information about a prior outcome. When prior outcomes were positive or absent people attributed more regret to action than to inaction, and following negative prior outcomes more regret was attributed to inaction, which they named the inaction effect. In medicine, Ayanian and Berwick surveyed paediatricians on case scenarios for three decisions. Given the subset of scenarios in which the initial reviewers were least likely to act, later physicians tended to be more active on the tympanostomy tube decision, p = 0.004, and on radiography, p = 0.076. Given the subset in which the initial reviewers were most likely to act, the later reviewers were neither more nor less likely to act.

replication.headline: A fresh sample of World Cup penalties found goalkeepers saving as well by jumping as by staying, so the flagship finding did not hold.
replication.detail: Singh and Mukherjee re-examined the claim on 292 on-target penalty kicks from men's World Cup matches between 1982 and 2022. Their published abstract reports that goalkeepers again jumped left or right more often and stayed in the centre less often, but that they had statistically similar chances of stopping the goal for both decisions. It also reports more kicks to the left and right than to the centre in that sample, which removes the premise that staying is the higher-value choice. They conclude that jumping is not a sub-optimal action, that a high frequency of jumping does not indicate an action bias, and that the goalkeepers were deciding competently. The paper is paywalled and these statements are read off its abstract, so no effect size or interval from it appears in the structured fields here. The replication tests the penalty-kick case, not the laboratory inaction effect and not the medical or environmental findings, none of which had a located repeat.

study.cite: Singh, R., & Mukherjee, S. (2026). Replication: No action 'Bias' among elite soccer goalkeepers during penalty kicks. Journal of Economic Psychology, 113, 102886.

limits: The centre option in the original rests on 18 kicks, of which 6 were stopped, and Table 2 attaches no interval to the 33.3 percent it reports. The authors state the conditional nature of their own advice: the argument that staying is better holds for the current distribution of kicks, and if goalkeepers always stayed, kickers would aim to the sides. They call the mixed-strategy equilibrium of the game beyond the scope of the article and leave it for future research, so the paper does not show that staying is optimal in equilibrium. The two sides are also not independent. Jump direction matched kick direction in 43 percent of kicks, above the 33.3 percent a goalkeeper could reach by choosing at random. The regret survey, which is the part that tests the proposed mechanism rather than the behaviour, missed the 5 percent threshold and lost half its sample to a ceiling. Roger David Berger circulated a comment on the study, "Should I stay or should I go? Optimal decision making in penalty kicks", on SSRN in 2009; its full text could not be retrieved, so nothing it argues is reported here. Patt and Zeckhauser's paper and Singh and Mukherjee's are both closed access and are quoted from their abstracts. Ayanian and Berwick is quoted from its PubMed abstract, which gives no result for the third decision they studied, emergency-room referral, and does not name the classic study it revisits. Searches of Crossref, OpenAlex and the open web for the same test in handball, ice hockey or any other sport found nothing.
misreadings: The saving rate people quote is the wrong one. Retellings give 60 percent as what a goalkeeper gets by staying put, and that figure is in Table 2, but it is the rate over the 10 kicks that went to the centre and met a goalkeeper who had stayed. A goalkeeper choosing before the kick cannot condition on where the ball will go. His number is 33.3 percent, six stops in eighteen. The second error is treating action bias and omission bias as rival findings that cannot both be true. Bar-Eli and colleagues answered that in their own abstract, which says the omission bias is reversed here because the norm here is reversed, to act rather than to choose inaction. Both entries describe one asymmetry running off normality, and Zeelenberg and colleagues show it turning direction inside a single set of experiments when the prior outcome changes. A corpus that lists both is not contradicting itself, though a reader who takes either as a standing preference will think it is. The third error is citing the penalty study as settled proof that experts stay irrational under high stakes. That was its selling point, and it is the claim the 2026 replication did not support.
